citation: Patterson D., Gonzalez J., Le Q., Liang C., Munguia L.-M., Rothchild D., So D., Texier M., Dean J. Carbon Emissions and Large Neural Network Training. arXiv:2104.10350.
venue: arXiv preprint (no journal reference listed on arXiv page)
evidence_class: B (accounting of real training runs; partly estimated)
research_question: How much energy and CO2e do large NN training runs use, and which choices (model, datacenter, processor, location/time) dominate?
method: Energy and carbon accounting for T5, Meena, GShard, Switch Transformer and GPT-3 using processor energy, datacenter PUE and grid carbon intensity; refines earlier Evolved Transformer NAS estimates.
hardware_workload: Large-model training on TPUs/GPUs in Google and other datacenters (per-model hardware details not re-verified here).
baseline: Dense models; typical (non-cloud) datacenters; off-the-shelf processors.
reported_results: Sparsely activated models can use under one tenth the energy of comparable dense models without accuracy loss; carbon-free energy share (hence CO2e) varies roughly 5-10x by location and time; cloud datacenters about 1.4-2x more energy-efficient than typical; ML accelerators about 2-5x more effective than off-the-shelf hardware; combined choices span roughly 100-1000x in footprint. Paper text gives PUE 1.11 for the Google Iowa datacenter vs a US average of 1.58 (2018) and 1.59 (2020).
limitations: Retrospective estimates relying on operator-reported data; training only; no per-request inference energy; no cooling-system detail beyond PUE.
reproducibility: Inputs tabulated in paper; underlying telemetry not public (not verified).
relevance_to_ueic: Shows facility overhead (PUE) and siting multiply IT energy, so a per-task metric must include facility energy, not GPU energy alone.
potential_implementation: Use PUE ~1.1 (efficient) vs ~1.6 (average) as facility-overhead scenarios; report energy and CO2e per successful task.
verified_how: Fetched arXiv abstract page (v3); PUE values read from alphaXiv rendering of the paper text (https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2104.10350.md).

citation: Luccioni A.S., Jernite Y., Strubell E. Power Hungry Processing: Watts Driving the Cost of AI Deployment? Proc. ACM FAccT '24. DOI 10.1145/3630106.3658542. arXiv:2311.16863.
venue: ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT '24), Rio de Janeiro
research_question: How does inference energy of task-specific models compare with general-purpose (multi-task generative) models?
method: Measure energy and carbon to run 1,000 inferences on representative benchmark datasets across many tasks and models.
hardware_workload: Inference across many tasks/models (exact counts and GPU type not stated in abstract; not verified).
reported_results: Multi-purpose generative architectures were reported as orders of magnitude more energy-expensive than task-specific systems across a variety of tasks, even when controlling for parameter count.
limitations: Abstract gives no absolute energy numbers; measurement boundary (GPU-only vs node) not verified; no facility/cooling overhead.
reproducibility: Data available through an interactive demo (per abstract).
relevance_to_ueic: Model choice can dominate infrastructure knobs; the routing module should include small task-specific models as options.
potential_implementation: Add specialized small models to the routing action space with per-inference energy priors.
verified_how: Fetched arXiv abstract page (v3).

citation: Samsi S., Zhao D., McDonald J., Li B., Michaleas A., Jones M., Bergeron W., Kepner J., Tiwari D., Gadepally V. From Words to Watts: Benchmarking the Energy Costs of Large Language Model Inference. arXiv:2310.03003.
venue: arXiv preprint; an IEEE Xplore record (document 10363447) appeared in search results but the conference venue was not verified
research_question: What are the compute and energy costs of LLM inference at multi-GPU scale, and how does GPU power capping affect them?
method: Benchmark LLaMA models of several sizes on V100 and A100 GPUs with Alpaca and GSM8K; sharded multi-node inference up to 32 GPUs; power-cap sweep.
hardware_workload: NVIDIA V100 and A100; LLaMA (several sizes incl. 65B); Alpaca, GSM8K.
baseline: Default 250 W A100 power limit (for capping experiment).
reported_results: Full text reports roughly 3-4 J per output token for LLaMA-65B (passage somewhat ambiguous about generation length). Capping A100s from 250 W to 175 W cut energy by about 23% on average with about 6.7% longer inference time; at 150 W time rose about 19.5% on average and energy fell about 33-35% (GSM8K, batch 64).
limitations: Described as preliminary; older GPUs; GPU-level energy only (boundary not verified); capping tested on one configuration.
relevance_to_ueic: Direct evidence that power caps trade modest latency for large GPU-energy savings in LLM inference, and lower power also means less heat to reject.
potential_implementation: Calibrate a power-cap -> (latency, energy) response curve for the compute model and use these points as validation targets.
verified_how: Fetched arXiv abstract page and ar5iv full-text HTML (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2310.03003).

workstream: AI energy measurement / GPU power management
citation: You J., Chung J.-W., Chowdhury M. Zeus: Understanding and Optimizing GPU Energy Consumption of DNN Training. 20th USENIX NSDI '23, pp. 119-139.
research_question: Can job- and GPU-level configuration be tuned online to cut DNN training energy, and what is the energy-time tradeoff?
method: Online exploration-exploitation with just-in-time energy profiling over batch size and GPU power limit for recurring jobs; cost = weighted mix of energy-to-accuracy and time-to-accuracy with user parameter eta.
hardware_workload: DNN training on NVIDIA GPUs (e.g., V100) across diverse workloads.
baseline: Default configurations (e.g., maximum power limit, default batch size).
reported_results: Energy efficiency improved by 15.3%-75.8% across workloads. Energy-optimal and time-optimal settings differ (example: DeepSpeech2 on V100, batch 32 at 100 W vs batch 48 at 250 W); feasible settings form a non-linear Pareto frontier.
limitations: Training of recurring jobs only; GPU energy only; no cooling or facility coupling.
reproducibility: A zeus-ml package appeared on PyPI in search results (not fetched; not verified).
relevance_to_ueic: Provides an eta-weighted energy-time objective and evidence that power limit is a non-linear knob, which is directly reusable for UEIC's compute actions.
potential_implementation: Adopt the eta-weighted cost form, extended with cooling energy; include power limit and batch size as actions.
verified_how: Fetched USENIX presentation page and NSDI paper PDF (https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi23-you.pdf).

workstream: AI energy measurement / GPU power management
citation: Chung J.-W., Gu Y., Jang I., Meng L., Bansal N., Chowdhury M. Reducing Energy Bloat in Large Model Training (system: Perseus). SOSP '24. DOI 10.1145/3694715.3695970. arXiv:2312.06902.
venue: ACM SIGOPS 30th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP '24), Austin TX
research_question: How much large-model training energy does not contribute to throughput, and can it be removed without slowdown?
method: Identify intrinsic bloat (computation imbalance across pipeline stages) and extrinsic bloat (stragglers among data-parallel pipelines); graph-cut algorithm computes the time-energy frontier; per-computation GPU SM frequency set via NVML.
hardware_workload: Large-model training (e.g., GPT-3, Bloom) on multi-GPU clusters.
reported_results: Reduces training energy by up to 30% with no throughput loss and no hardware modification.
limitations: Pipeline-parallel training; GPU energy only; cooling not considered.
relevance_to_ueic: Slack-aware frequency planning removes energy (and heat) from off-critical-path work at zero slowdown, which is a core UEIC scheduling primitive.
potential_implementation: Implement slack-aware per-stage frequency assignment in simulated multi-GPU jobs; feed the resulting heat profile to the cooling model.
verified_how: Fetched arXiv abstract page (v3) and arXiv HTML v3 (venue line, mechanism).

citation: Chung J.-W., Ma J.J., Wu R., Liu J., Kweon O.J., Xia Y., Wu Z., Chowdhury M. The ML.ENERGY Benchmark: Toward Automated Inference Energy Measurement and Optimization. NeurIPS 2025 (spotlight poster). arXiv:2505.06371.
research_question: How can inference energy be measured under realistic serving conditions and optimized automatically?
method: Benchmark suite and tool following four design principles; public leaderboard; automated optimization recommendations.
hardware_workload: 40 widely used model architectures across 6 tasks (early-2025 iteration); GPU types not verified.
reported_results: Automated recommendations reduce energy, sometimes by more than 40%, without changing what the model computes.
limitations: GPU-level measurement (facility overhead not verified); recommendations are serving-configuration level only.
reproducibility: Open source and extensible to custom models (per abstract).
relevance_to_ueic: Source of per-model inference energy priors and a measurement methodology to align UEIC's compute model with.
potential_implementation: Import leaderboard energy-per-request values as priors for the routing module (data license and format not verified).
verified_how: Fetched arXiv abstract page and NeurIPS 2025 virtual poster page.

citation: Elsworth C., Huang K., Patterson D., Schneider I., Sedivy R., Goodman S., Townsend B., Ranganathan P., Dean J., Vahdat A., Gomes B., Manyika J. Measuring the environmental impact of delivering AI at Google Scale. arXiv:2508.15734.
research_question: What are the energy, carbon and water costs of AI serving measured in production, with a full-stack boundary?
method: Production measurement methodology applied to Gemini serving; boundary includes active accelerator power, host system energy, idle machine capacity and datacenter energy overhead.
hardware_workload: Google production serving infrastructure for Gemini Apps text prompts.
baseline: Public estimates; the same service one year earlier.
reported_results: Median Gemini Apps text prompt: 0.24 Wh and about 0.26 mL of water. Over one year, software efficiency and clean-energy procurement gave 33x lower energy and 44x lower carbon per median prompt.
limitations: Self-reported by operator; not externally reproducible; median-prompt definition; not peer reviewed.
relevance_to_ueic: Defines a boundary (accelerator + host + idle capacity + facility overhead) that matches UEIC's facility-energy-per-successful-task metric.
potential_implementation: Adopt the same boundary in UEIC accounting; use 0.24 Wh as an order-of-magnitude sanity check, not a target.
verified_how: Fetched arXiv abstract page.

citation: Tang Z., Wang Y., Wang Q., Chu X. The Impact of GPU DVFS on the Energy and Performance of Deep Learning: an Empirical Study. arXiv:1905.11012.
research_question: How does GPU core frequency scaling affect DNN training and inference energy and performance?
method: Empirical sweeps of GPU core frequency across DNNs and batch sizes.
hardware_workload: Tesla P100, Tesla V100, GTX 2080Ti; AlexNet, VGG-16, GoogLeNet, ResNet-50.
reported_results: Optimal core frequency saved 8.7%-23.1% energy for training and 19.6%-26.4% for inference vs default settings.
limitations: CNNs only; older GPUs; GPU power only; no thermal or cooling measurements.
relevance_to_ueic: Confirms a workload-dependent energy-optimal clock, i.e. maximum clock is generally not energy-optimal.
potential_implementation: Use as a sanity check for the shape of the simulated frequency-energy curve.
verified_how: Fetched arXiv abstract page.

citation: Maliakel P.J., Ilager S., Brandic I. Characterizing LLM Inference Energy-Performance Tradeoffs across Workloads and GPU Scaling. arXiv:2501.08219 (v4, 2026).
venue: arXiv preprint (v4 dated Feb 2026; no venue stated)
research_question: How do prefill (compute-bound) and decode (memory-bound) phases of LLM inference respond to GPU frequency scaling?
method: Sweep seven SM frequencies (180-2842 MHz) across five decoder-only LLMs and four NLP benchmarks; offline single-GPU replay.
hardware_workload: Single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (Blackwell); LLMs 1B-32B.
reported_results: Decode takes 77-91% of inference time, is memory-bound and its latency changes by under 1% across frequencies; prefill is compute-bound with latency up about 7-26% at 180 MHz. At 180 MHz GPU energy fell about 42% on average with end-to-end latency up about 1-3% (abstract states 1-6%). Savings plateau below roughly 1000 MHz; EDP optimum near 960 MHz for most models at batch 1.
limitations: Preprint; offline replay; one workstation-class GPU; GPU-only energy; internal inconsistency on latency figure.
relevance_to_ueic: Strongest verified evidence that memory-bound decode is nearly clock-insensitive, so phase-aware DVFS can cut GPU power (and heat load) with little latency cost.
potential_implementation: Model separate prefill/decode frequency-latency-power curves; allow per-phase clock actions.
verified_how: Fetched arXiv abstract page (tool returned full-text details).

citation: Patel P., Choukse E., Zhang C., Goiri I., Warrier B., Mahalingam N., Bianchini R. Characterizing Power Management Opportunities for LLMs in the Cloud. ASPLOS '24. Preprint titled: POLCA: Power Oversubscription in LLM Cloud Providers, arXiv:2308.12908 (2023).
evidence_class: B (power characterization); C (POLCA evaluated in simulation)
research_question: What are LLM training/inference power patterns, and can LLM inference clusters be power-oversubscribed safely?
method: Characterize power of open-source LLMs under common configurations; evaluate GPU frequency locking and power capping; simulate the POLCA oversubscription framework with open-source models replaying production power patterns.
hardware_workload: Open-source LLMs (e.g., BLOOM, GPT-NeoX, Flan-T5) on datacenter GPU servers (exact GPU not verified).
reported_results: Inference average and peak power are fairly low, leaving oversubscription headroom. For inference, frequency locking reclaimed up to about 20% of peak power for up to about 7% performance loss (model dependent). Power capping is reactive, so short prompt-phase spikes near or above TDP can exceed caps; token phases are longer and lower power. For training, frequency locking cut peak server power 22% at about 10% performance cost. Simulation: about 30% more servers in existing clusters with minimal throttling.
limitations: Oversubscription results are simulated; open-source models used as proxies for production.
relevance_to_ueic: Establishes the phase structure of LLM power and the different behavior of frequency locking vs power capping, both candidate UEIC actuators.
potential_implementation: Model prompt/token power phases; compare frequency-lock and power-cap actuators in the compute model.
verified_how: Fetched author-hosted ASPLOS PDF, Microsoft Research publication page, and arXiv abstract of POLCA preprint (https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.12908v1).

citation: Patel P., Choukse E., Zhang C., Shah A., Goiri I., Maleki S., Bianchini R. Splitwise: Efficient generative LLM inference using phase splitting. ISCA 2024. arXiv:2311.18677.
evidence_class: B (phase characterization); cluster-level evaluation method not verified
research_question: Can splitting prompt and token-generation phases onto separate machines improve throughput, cost and power efficiency?
method: Characterize the two phases; design homogeneous and heterogeneous clusters with state transfer over cluster interconnects.
hardware_workload: Generative LLM inference on GPU clusters.
reported_results: Prompt phase is compute-intensive; token generation is memory-intensive, underuses compute and can run on cheaper, lower-power hardware. Reported up to 1.4x throughput at 20% lower cost, or up to 2.35x throughput under the same power and cost budgets.
limitations: Requires fast interconnect for state transfer; cooling not considered.
relevance_to_ueic: Disaggregated phases create machine pools with distinct power densities, which could be cooled at different setpoints.
potential_implementation: Simulate separate prefill and decode pools with pool-specific DVFS and coolant setpoints.
verified_how: Fetched Microsoft Research publication page.

citation: Stojkovic J., Zhang C., Goiri I., Torrellas J., Choukse E. DynamoLLM: Designing LLM Inference Clusters for Performance and Energy Efficiency. HPCA 2025 (DOI 10.1109/HPCA61900.2025.00102 per arXiv page). arXiv:2408.00741.
venue: IEEE HPCA 2025 (from DOI shown on arXiv page)
evidence_class: B or C (whether headline results are from real cluster or simulation not verified)
research_question: Can LLM inference clusters be reconfigured over time to cut energy while meeting latency SLOs?
method: Energy-management framework exploiting workload heterogeneity and load fluctuation; reconfigures number of instances, model parallelism and GPU frequency.
hardware_workload: LLM inference clusters (GPU type not verified).
reported_results: At service level, about 53% energy savings, 38% lower operational carbon and 61% lower customer cost while meeting latency SLOs.
limitations: Cooling and facility energy not modeled (per abstract); evaluation setup not verified.
relevance_to_ueic: Closest compute-side analogue of UEIC: joint reconfiguration plus GPU frequency under SLOs.
potential_implementation: Use as the compute-only baseline that UEIC's joint compute+cooling controller must beat.
verified_how: Fetched arXiv abstract page.

citation: Stojkovic J., Zhang C., Goiri I., Choukse E., Qiu H., Fonseca R., Torrellas J., Bianchini R. TAPAS: Thermal- and Power-Aware Scheduling for LLM Inference in Cloud Platforms. ASPLOS '25. arXiv:2501.02600.
research_question: Can thermal- and power-aware placement, routing and reconfiguration of LLM inference raise cooling/power oversubscription and handle emergencies?
method: Regression models: server inlet temperature vs outside temperature and datacenter load; GPU temperature vs inlet temperature and GPU load (MAE under 1 C). Policies: VM placement, request routing, reconfiguration (parallelism, model size, quantization).
hardware_workload: Large GPU cluster for LLM inference (air-side inlet temperatures modeled).
reported_results: Maximum temperature reduced 17% and peak row power 23% while keeping P99 latency; up to 40% extra capacity via oversubscription; thermal throttling events down 97% and power throttling down 99% vs other practical policies in trace-based simulation.
limitations: Simulation-based; air-cooling context (applicability to liquid cooling not stated); does not optimize the cooling plant itself.
relevance_to_ueic: Closest published thermal-aware LLM scheduler; shows GPU temperature depends jointly on load and inlet temperature, which is the coupling UEIC exploits.
potential_implementation: Reuse the GPU-temperature = f(inlet temperature, load) regression structure, replacing air inlet with coolant supply temperature.
verified_how: Fetched arXiv abstract, arXiv HTML v1, Microsoft Research page, and UIUC course-hosted PDF for venue line (https://courses.grainger.illinois.edu/CS533/sp2026/reading_list/13b.pdf).

citation: Horowitz M. 1.1 Computing's Energy Problem (and what we can do about it). IEEE ISSCC 2014, Digest of Technical Papers, Session 1 Plenary.
research_question: Where does energy go in modern computing, and what can reduce it after the end of Dennard scaling?
method: Plenary analysis of per-operation energies in a 45 nm, 0.9 V process and their implications for architecture.
hardware_workload: Generic CMOS logic, SRAM and DRAM at 45 nm.
reported_results: Body text states roughly 1-2 nJ per DRAM access, about 10 pJ for an internal cache access or functional operation, about 20 pJ per cache fetch and about 70 pJ per processor instruction. Figure 1.1.9 tabulates per-operation energies but its numbers were illegible in the fetched copies (see L15 for a verified reproduction).
limitations: 45 nm technology; order-of-magnitude figures; modern HBM and advanced nodes differ.
relevance_to_ueic: Data movement dominates arithmetic energy, so memory-bound phases (decode) are energy-dominated by memory traffic rather than FLOPs.
potential_implementation: Energy model E = N_ops*e_op + N_bytes*e_mem with technology-scaled coefficients.
verified_how: Fetched two hosted PDFs (UW-Madison course page; https://www.Gwern.net/doc/cs/hardware/2014-horowitz-2.pdf); figure values not legible.

citation: Han S., Pool J., Tran J., Dally W.J. Learning both Weights and Connections for Efficient Neural Networks. NeurIPS 2015, pp. 1135-1143. arXiv:1506.02626.
evidence_class: B (secondary reproduction of Horowitz 45 nm energy table)
research_question: (Main topic: pruning.) Used here only for its reproduction of the 45 nm per-operation energy table.
method: Figure 1 table citing Horowitz, 'Energy table for 45nm process'.
hardware_workload: 45 nm CMOS.
reported_results: 32-bit int add 0.1 pJ; float add 0.9 pJ; register file 1 pJ; int multiply 3.1 pJ; float multiply 3.7 pJ; SRAM cache 5 pJ; DRAM 640 pJ (about 6400x an int add). Pruning results of the paper were not checked.
limitations: Secondary citation; 45 nm values; not representative of HBM3 at modern nodes.
relevance_to_ueic: Verified numerical basis for the DRAM-vs-arithmetic energy ratio used in the compute model.
potential_implementation: Seed e_op and e_mem coefficients; scale to modern nodes as an explicit class-E extrapolation.
verified_how: Fetched arXiv PDF and ML Anthology listing (https://mlanthology.org/neurips/2015/han2015neurips-learning).

citation: Williams S., Waterman A., Patterson D. Roofline: an insightful visual performance model for multicore architectures. Communications of the ACM 52(4):65-76.
evidence_class: A (established analytical performance model; not a physical law)
research_question: How can attainable performance be bounded by compute peak and memory bandwidth?
method: Analytical bound: attainable FLOP/s = min(peak FLOP/s, peak memory bandwidth x operational intensity), intensity in FLOPs per byte of DRAM traffic.
hardware_workload: Multicore architectures (general).
reported_results: Defines operational intensity (FLOPs/byte of DRAM traffic) and the min() roofline bound.
limitations: Ignores latency, contention and power/thermal limits.
relevance_to_ueic: First-principles classification of prefill (high intensity) vs decode (low intensity), predicting which phases are clock-sensitive.
potential_implementation: Use roofline to set the compute vs memory time split in the DVFS latency model.
verified_how: Fetched Crossref API record and course-hosted CACM PDF (https://www.cs.colostate.edu/~cs475/f19/more_assignments/Labs/L10/RooflineCACM2009.pdf).

citation: Leviathan Y., Kalman M., Matias Y. Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding. Proc. 40th ICML, PMLR 202:19274-19286.
research_question: Can autoregressive sampling be accelerated without changing the output distribution?
method: A smaller approximation model drafts tokens; the large model verifies them in parallel; novel sampling keeps the large model's distribution.
hardware_workload: T5-XXL (TPU/accelerator details not verified).
reported_results: 2x-3x speedup on T5-XXL with identical outputs; no retraining or architecture change.
limitations: Energy not reported in abstract; gains depend on draft acceptance rate.
relevance_to_ueic: Converts many sequential memory-bound passes into fewer verification passes; energy benefit is plausible but unmeasured here (treat as class F until measured).
potential_implementation: Optional decode-acceleration mode in the compute model with acceptance-rate parameter.
verified_how: Fetched PMLR proceedings page.

citation: Dao T., Fu D.Y., Ermon S., Rudra A., Re C. FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness. NeurIPS 2022. arXiv:2205.14135.
research_question: Can exact attention be made faster by minimizing GPU memory traffic?
method: IO-aware tiling to reduce reads/writes between HBM and on-chip SRAM.
hardware_workload: GPU training/inference of Transformers (GPT-2, Long-Range Arena).
reported_results: 3x speedup on GPT-2 (sequence length 1K) and 2.4x on Long-Range Arena (1K-4K).
limitations: Energy not reported in abstract.
relevance_to_ueic: Reducing HBM traffic targets the dominant energy term identified by L14/L15.
potential_implementation: Represent as reduced bytes-moved in the attention kernel model.
verified_how: Fetched NeurIPS proceedings abstract page.

citation: Dettmers T., Lewis M., Belkada Y., Zettlemoyer L. LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale. arXiv:2208.07339. Listed in NeurIPS 2022 proceedings as 'GPT3.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale'.
research_question: Can large transformers run inference with 8-bit matrix multiplication without accuracy loss?
method: Vector-wise quantization plus mixed-precision decomposition that keeps systematic outlier dimensions in 16-bit.
hardware_workload: Transformer LMs up to 175B parameters (e.g., OPT-175B, BLOOM).
reported_results: Roughly halves inference memory while keeping full-precision performance up to 175B parameters; more than 99.9% of values are multiplied in 8-bit.
limitations: Speed and energy not quantified in abstract.
relevance_to_ueic: Lower-precision weights reduce memory traffic in memory-bound decode; a model-variant option for routing.
potential_implementation: Model INT8 variants with reduced bytes per token and an accuracy-retention parameter.
verified_how: Fetched arXiv abstract page and ML Anthology page (https://mlanthology.org/neurips/2022/dettmers2022neurips-gpt3).

citation: Frantar E., Ashkboos S., Hoefler T., Alistarh D. GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers. ICLR 2023. arXiv:2210.17323.
research_question: Can GPT-scale models be quantized to 3-4 bits in one shot with little accuracy loss?
method: One-shot weight quantization using approximate second-order information.
hardware_workload: Models up to 175B parameters; NVIDIA A100 and A6000.
baseline: FP16 inference; prior one-shot quantization methods.
reported_results: Quantizes a 175B model in about four GPU hours to 3-4 bits with negligible accuracy loss; enables 175B inference on a single GPU; about 3.25x (A100) and 4.5x (A6000) speedups over FP16.
limitations: Energy not reported in abstract; weight-only quantization.
reproducibility: Code public at github.com/IST-DASLab/gptq (per arXiv page).
relevance_to_ueic: Speedups for memory-bound generation imply less energy per token; candidate low-energy model variants.
potential_implementation: Add 4-bit variants to routing with speedup and accuracy parameters.
verified_how: Fetched arXiv abstract page and T. Hoefler publication page (https://www.unixer.de/publications/index.php?pub=477).

citation: Fedus W., Zoph B., Shazeer N. Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity. JMLR 23(120):1-39. arXiv:2101.03961 (2021).
research_question: Can a simplified mixture-of-experts scale parameters while keeping compute per token constant?
method: Simplified top-1 routing MoE with improved training techniques; bfloat16 training of sparse models.
hardware_workload: Pre-training on C4 (TPU details not verified).
reported_results: Up to 7x pre-training speedup over T5-Base/Large with the same compute; 4x speedup over T5-XXL; gains over mT5-Base in all 101 languages; models up to a trillion parameters.
limitations: Memory footprint and communication; inference energy not in abstract.
relevance_to_ueic: Sparse activation decouples parameter count from FLOPs per token; L01 reports large energy savings for sparse models.
potential_implementation: Represent MoE models by active vs total parameters in the routing module.
verified_how: Fetched JMLR paper page.

citation: Chen L., Zaharia M., Zou J. FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance. TMLR 2024. arXiv:2305.05176 (2023).
research_question: Can per-query selection among LLM APIs cut cost while maintaining or improving accuracy?
method: Prompt adaptation, LLM approximation and LLM cascade; FrugalGPT learns which LLMs to use per query.
hardware_workload: Commercial LLM APIs; news classification, reading comprehension, scientific QA.
reported_results: Matches GPT-4 with up to 98% cost reduction, or improves accuracy by 4% at the same cost.
limitations: Optimizes API dollar cost, not energy; mapping cost to energy is an extrapolation (class E).
relevance_to_ueic: Cascades reduce large-model calls per successful task, directly lowering the numerator of UEIC's metric.
potential_implementation: Implement a cascade router with per-model energy and success-probability priors.
verified_how: Fetched ML Anthology page and arXiv abstract v1 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.05176v1).

citation: Lazic N., Lu T., Boutilier C., Ryu M.K., Wong E.J., Roy B., Imwalle G. Data center cooling using model-predictive control. NeurIPS 2018, pp. 3818-3827.
research_question: Can a learned model-predictive controller safely regulate a large data center server floor more efficiently than local PID control?
method: Linear ARX model learned from about 3 hours of randomized exploration; MPC sets AHU fan speed and water valve; regulates cold-aisle temperature and differential pressure; server power and entering water temperature treated as disturbances.
hardware_workload: Air-handling units on a large Google data center floor.
reported_results: MPC was more efficient than local controllers in all conditions except low entering water temperature with low server load; authors estimate potential savings of about 9% of server-floor cooling cost, noting longer experiments are needed to confirm.
limitations: Air-side only; short trial (one day vs a week of PID data); cost proxy; server power treated as exogenous.
relevance_to_ueic: Demonstrates safe learned MPC on a real cooling plant; UEIC extends it by making IT power a decision variable rather than a disturbance.
potential_implementation: Template for the cooling controller: ARX or similar model + receding-horizon optimization with exploration phase.
verified_how: Fetched Google Research page and NeurIPS paper PDF (https://papers.NeurIPS.cc/paper_files/paper/2018/file/059fdcd96baeb75112f09fa1dcc740cc-Paper.pdf).

citation: Parolini L., Sinopoli B., Krogh B.H., Wang Z. A Cyber-Physical-System Approach to Data Center Modeling and Control for Energy Efficiency. Proceedings of the IEEE (special issue on CPS), Dec 2011; volume/pages not verified.
research_question: Does coordinating IT (computational) and cooling (thermal) control save energy relative to independent control?
method: Coupled computational and thermal network model; compares baseline, uncoordinated and coordinated control strategies.
hardware_workload: Simulated data center.

evidence_class: B/C (V100 profiling with Llama-2 7B plus simulation on Azure traces; split not verified)
research_question: Can hierarchical co-optimisation of GPU parallelism, DVFS and cooling cut LLM-serving energy while keeping GPUs thermally safe?
method: Four timescales: LSTM capacity sizing (30 min), MILP tensor-parallel selection (5 min), cooling MPC on supply air temperature and airflow (60 s) over state-space rack thermal dynamics, per-job DVFS under latency, energy and temperature constraints
hardware_workload: Air-cooled racks with rack cooling units; 8x Tesla V100, Llama-2 7B; Azure LLM inference traces
baseline: PID cooling and others (details not read)
reported_results: 24.2% computing-energy and 31.2% cooling-energy savings, 17.0% lower mean GPU temperature, negligible latency impact (paper's claims)
limitations: Air cooling only; older GPU and one model; ramp or actuator rate limits not mentioned in the text read; MPC details truncated in the fetched text
relevance_to_ueic: Prior art for joint DVFS + cooling MPC with thermal dynamics for LLM serving. UEIC's slow-loop work differs in cooling type (facility liquid loop with ramp-limited plant) and in testing a model-free alternative
potential_implementation: Its timescale split could structure a UEIC controller with routing and capacity sizing
